items.title: When 'iel' entered Le Robert
items.claim: Le Robert added the gender-neutral pronoun 'iel' (combining il and elle) to its online edition in which year?
items.reveal:
The inclusion drew commentary from the Education Minister and politicians. The Academie francaise has been sceptical of inclusive writing more broadly.

Dictionaries describe usage rather than prescribe it.
items.why: Dictionary inclusions of contested terms become flashpoints in language politics.

items.title: Loi Toubon
items.claim: France's loi Toubon (1994) requires French in certain official contexts. Which is closest to what it covers?

options.text: It bans English speech in private homes
It requires French in commercial advertising, employment contracts and public-sector communication, with alternatives in foreign languages permitted but a French version also required
It applies only to government emails
It applies only to broadcast television

items.reveal_title: It mandates French in public commercial and administrative contexts
items.reveal:
The law was originally proposed by Jacques Toubon (then Minister of Culture). Some clauses were softened by the Constitutional Council on freedom-of-expression grounds.

Enforcement is sporadic but has produced occasional fines.
items.why: Language policy is most visible at the interface between commerce and state.

items.title: Camus and Nobel age
items.claim: When Albert Camus won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1957, he was the second-youngest laureate at the time. About what age?
items.reveal:
Camus published L'Etranger in 1942 and La Peste in 1947. He died in a car accident on 4 January 1960.

Rudyard Kipling at 41 was younger when he won in 1907.
items.why: Award timing is shaped by the political and editorial currents of its decade.
